eras.name: Founder's Era

periods.name: Frontier Settlement
periods.summary: A landing, a mill, and a few cabins mark the beginning of a town. Beyond them lie the woods and the promise of a new settlement.
suggestions: Choose a dry site near water and timber.
Lay out a short route between the landing and the first workshops.

periods.name: Colonial Growth
periods.summary: The settlement finds its footing. Farms send their harvests to market, and workshops fill the streets leading down to the wharf.
suggestions: Connect farms to mills and markets.
Make room for shops along the busiest streets.

periods.name: A New Nation
periods.summary: A new nation must supply itself. Local trades take on work once carried across the ocean, while merchants seek routes of their own.
suggestions: Strengthen local processing and repair trades.
Connect trading settlements by road and water.

periods.name: Early Republic
periods.summary: Market towns push inland. More people, produce, and timber move along the rivers, and inland roads begin to carry heavier traffic.
suggestions: Extend roads toward productive land.
Reserve waterfront sites for loading and receiving goods.

eras.summary: Your nation takes root at the water’s edge. Cabins give way to market streets, and roads carry the first goods between settlements.
suggestions: Settle near timber, farmland, and dependable water access.
Link workshops and landing places to the town center.

eras.name: Industrial Era

periods.name: Transportation Revolution
periods.summary: Canals and early railroads cut new paths across the country. Steam starts to carry goods farther than a wagon team could take them.
suggestions: Reserve a route from freight landings to mills.
Keep space for roads alongside major transport corridors.

periods.name: Industrial Expansion
periods.summary: The mill town grows into a factory town. Its workshops need more workers, more raw materials, and a dependable way to get goods to market.
suggestions: Cluster related processors and workshops.
Connect workers’ neighborhoods to industrial streets.

periods.name: Transformation
periods.summary: Rail and steam bring larger factories within reach. Towns at the junction of trade routes begin to shape what their regions produce.
suggestions: Leave expansion room near major freight routes.
Separate heavy through traffic from local streets.

eras.summary: Your nation lays down railroads and puts steam to work. Mills and foundries draw small towns into a growing network of trade.
suggestions: Reserve corridors linking industry to the waterfront and future rail yards.
Place processing lots close to their raw materials.

eras.name: Victorian Era

periods.name: Railroad City
periods.summary: The depot becomes a new center of town life. A rail connection can turn a local workshop into a supplier for an entire region.
suggestions: Reserve room for freight handling near depots.
Connect warehouses to industrial streets.

periods.name: Urban Boom
periods.summary: New streets fill with houses and storefronts. Workshops and rail yards take on the work of supplying a fast-growing city.
suggestions: Extend services toward new neighborhoods.
Keep deliveries accessible behind busy commercial streets.

periods.name: Metropolitan Age
periods.summary: The city reaches beyond any one district. Its stations, markets, streets, and harbor must move people and goods together.
suggestions: Strengthen links between districts.
Reserve land near major junctions for commerce and freight.

eras.summary: Rail lines bind the nation together as towns swell into cities. Depots, workshops, and crowded market streets set the pace of urban life.
suggestions: Leave room around stations for freight and commerce.
Extend streets ahead of growing neighborhoods.

eras.name: Machine Age

periods.name: New Century
periods.summary: The new century brings faster machinery and bigger markets. Old workshops adapt while factories and warehouses fill the blocks around them.
suggestions: Connect production sites to regional freight routes.
Keep local repair shops near the industries they serve.

periods.name: Motor Age Begins
periods.summary: Motor vehicles begin to share the road with horses. Streets built for local journeys take on longer trips and heavier loads.
suggestions: Plan wider routes where freight traffic converges.
Leave maneuvering space at loading areas.

eras.summary: Engines promise to change who can travel, how far they can go, and how quickly goods reach market. The city begins to make room for the motor age.
suggestions: Reserve routes for traffic between workshops and commercial streets.
Keep new industrial sites accessible from more than one direction.

eras.name: Art Deco Era

periods.name: Roaring Twenties
periods.summary: Shops, workshops, and traffic fill the city streets. Growing demand reaches from the factory floor to the newest outlying neighborhoods.
suggestions: Link new housing to established commercial streets.
Keep loading access available as storefronts multiply.

periods.name: Depression Era
periods.summary: Hard times change what the city needs. Repair and reuse matter more as households and businesses make existing buildings and equipment last.
suggestions: Prioritize maintenance and adaptable workshops.
Make use of streets and services already in place.

periods.name: Wartime City
periods.summary: Wartime work puts ports, factories, and repair shops under pressure. Moving supplies reliably becomes as important as producing them.
suggestions: Give ports and industrial yards dependable road access.
Keep alternative routes available for essential freight.

eras.summary: Bold skylines, busy harbors, and electric light mark a new age. Establish your City Center, connect homes and businesses, and build streets for a growing city—from the roaring twenties to wartime.
suggestions: Keep essential industries connected to reliable supply routes.
Reserve sites for repair shops and future production.

eras.name: Postwar Era

periods.name: Postwar Boom
periods.summary: Homebuilding surges and factories turn to peacetime goods. The city must house new families while its industry finds new markets.
suggestions: Support building-material suppliers near freight routes.
Connect new homes to established jobs and shops.

periods.name: Suburban Expansion
periods.summary: New neighborhoods spread beyond the old street grid. Longer trips change where shops and services can thrive.
suggestions: Plan routes between suburbs and town centers.
Reserve land for neighborhood shops near growing populations.

periods.name: Urban Transformation
periods.summary: The city weighs renewal against the cost of losing familiar streets. Former industrial sites and older neighborhoods face new uses.
suggestions: Look for vacant or underused sites near services.
Keep useful links between established neighborhoods.

eras.summary: New homes spread beyond the old city as highways carry workers and freight farther than before. The center must find its place in a larger metropolis.
suggestions: Plan connections between new neighborhoods and established job centers.
Keep through freight clear of local shopping streets.

eras.name: Contemporary Era

periods.name: Reinvention
periods.summary: Former industrial districts face a choice about what comes next. Workshops, warehouses, and waterfronts can find new work as the city changes around them.
suggestions: Reuse well-connected industrial sites.
Keep room for small workshops and specialty production.

periods.name: Information Age
periods.summary: Information travels faster than freight, but goods still need roads, ports, and warehouses. New businesses look for places connected to both.
suggestions: Choose sites with dependable access to regional markets.
Reuse older buildings where their locations still serve the city.

periods.name: New Millennium
periods.summary: Established cities return to their centers and waterfronts. New housing and commerce share streets built for older patterns of work.
suggestions: Connect redevelopment to existing streets and services.
Preserve working freight access where it is still needed.

periods.name: Connected City
periods.summary: Orders and deliveries can be coordinated across the city. Freight routes and local streets must handle more frequent journeys.
suggestions: Plan loading access away from busy pedestrian routes.
Connect distribution sites to more than one major road.

periods.name: Twenty-First Century City
periods.summary: The city must make room for new homes and industries while facing a changing climate. Its future depends on what it can reuse, reconnect, and protect.
suggestions: Keep new development away from vulnerable low ground.
Reuse established streets and sites to limit unnecessary expansion.

eras.summary: Old industrial ground takes on new purposes. Your cities rebuild around changing industries, renewed waterfronts, and a growing demand for connections.
suggestions: Look for industrial sites that can be reused near existing roads.
Preserve useful freight links while opening room for mixed development.
